title: After the 10,000-worker factory vanished, he had 20 years of workers' daily life on camera
dek: Others photographed the era's anomalies; he insisted on its ordinary days — meals, punch-ins, English classes. When the giant factory finally disappeared, only a handful of people had kept this archive.
why: Not an industry analysis — a migrant worker using a camera to write a biography of himself and his generation. The second half, on ‘density’ and ‘autoethnography’, is the most valuable part.
who: Founders and content people interested in manufacturing's transformation, documentary photography, and the situation of migrant workers; anyone who wants to understand how the Pearl River Delta factory era disappeared.
skip: The show promo and event notices at the start, 0:00-1:08, can be skipped.

points.h: The logic of the assembly line is to make a person's value unimportant
points.body: After the Foxconn suicides, Zhan Youbing was asked what he thought. He said he had seriously considered it: every assembly-line method works by subdividing the process to make manufacturing more stable and workers more replaceable. Translated, those two sentences mean — anyone can do it, and anyone will do it just as well. Though the machines had not yet replaced people, a person's value was already almost unimportant. This was the underlying motive for his later picking up a camera and aiming it at his fellow workers: inside a system deliberately flattening individual difference, to record specific people.

points.h: Riding the green-skin train felt like riding into a bandit's den
points.body: In 1995, after leaving the army, he went south. The carriage was already full at the Wuchang origin station — people above the seats, people below, people sleeping on the luggage racks, people everywhere in the toilets and the gangways between cars. At Chenzhou someone smashed the glass with a brick and shoved people onto the train like livestock. For more than thirty hours he could not sit or drink water; after getting off, his abdomen was badly swollen. At the Guangzhou railway station he was then cheated by touts into being ‘sold as a piglet’ — first they took over twenty yuan and said it was for Dongguan, then on the highway they demanded another ten for the expressway fee, and if you refused someone came up and slapped you, and finally they dumped you in a wasteland with no village ahead and no shop behind to change vehicles. He said he had used the term for years and only understood what it meant last year.

points.h: He did 102 push-ups for a security guard job
points.body: In 1995 finding work was hard, and men had a far harder time than women — factory recruitment notices stated outright that they only hired female workers aged 18 to 25. By the side of National Highway 107 he saw a hiring notice; the security captain had all the applicants lie down in the parking lot and do push-ups to screen their stamina. The count was drawn out long; by 20 people began to drop, by 40 only eight or ten were left, by 50-something only he remained. The captain said you're bragging, go ahead, and he did 102. After getting up he was told to spar with someone; the other man did a split, and he turned sideways, caught the leg and flipped him. That was how he got his first job: security guard at a hotel gate, 450 yuan a month.

points.h: An 1,800-yuan camera and 48-yuan rolls of film
points.body: In 2002 he struggled with the decision for a long time before buying his own camera: his wage was only around 1,500, he already had a child, and his wife was still back home. He called to discuss it, and his wife said if you like it, buy it. The camera was 1,800 yuan; film, even bought ten rolls at a time wholesale, was 48 each, plus 5 for developing and another ten or twenty for prints — in that era an enormous expense for him. At first he shot factory events, guest visits, employee tug-of-war, assuming that photography was just a matter of technique and clear images. Later, reading Chinese photography magazines, he discovered how much learning there was in photography and that he had no standard of measure, so he bought the New York Institute of Photography textbook, whose first lesson was the three criteria of a good photograph.

points.h: A model-contest photo passed ten million clicks, then he was told to delete it
points.body: In 2007 the factory began holding model contests; workers went on stage in swimsuits, evening gowns and uniforms, and there was pole dancing. In 2008 he changed his camera position, went to the stage backdrop and shot downward — models in front, a dense black mass of audience in the distance — and sent it promptly to Tencent, which put it on its portal site, and in one morning it got tens of millions of clicks. But online comments said this was choosing a mistress for the boss and a lover for the factory director; the public opinion was distorted, the boss came under huge pressure, and he was told to delete it. Tencent said it could only be hidden, other sites' viral reposting could not be stopped, and in the end he was given a notice reserving the right to pursue the matter.

points.h: That photo of the female worker looking up — he had not planned to use it
points.body: On January 5, 2011, as a senior supervisor, he entered the clean room to inspect fire safety, and because the work required it he openly brought his camera. After two hours of work in the clean room there was a four-minute break; the place where workers changed was hung with unused clean-room suits, and two people sat in front, one of them a fellow Hubei native. He pressed the shutter once or twice, and his fellow townsman heard the sound and looked up at him. He said the advice he had been given when learning photography was that ‘photos where the subject looks at the lens are not good photos’, so he had long avoided using this one. Later, Ren Yue, a teacher at Renmin University of China, organized the Off-Pix award; he submitted it, and it was unexpectedly used as the lead image. Looking at it seriously afterward, he admitted it had its own attraction — different readers would have different inner responses, so a photographer should interpret his photos as little as possible.

points.h: One set of ID papers lent to many people; after social security went online, his seniority was zeroed out
points.body: When he came out to find work in 1995, Hubei people were not wanted, Henan people were not wanted, Anhui people were acceptable, so he borrowed an Anhui man's ID card. At the time factories' information was separate, there was no networked computer system, and the social security system did not require contributions, so this set of papers was lent to many people and entered many factories. But after 2000 social security began to be networked, and the system did not recognize it — same ID number, same name, same household registration address — and the enterprise, feeling you were dishonest, zeroed out your years of service. He said this won't do; our generation is about to reach retirement age, and those years of service are real. When even present life is insecure, it is simply impossible to think about retirement twenty or fifty years away.

points.h: Density: he photographed for 20 years before discovering it was everywhere
points.body: In 2019 he curated a set of photographs around the thread of dense migrant-worker life, which won the Excellence Award and the Alpa Award at the third Hard Instant Image Awards. Workers' gatherings shot from high above, heads packed with almost no gaps; collective dormitories hung with clothes that from a distance looked airtight; workshop switches, key cabinets, lockers holding bowls and chopsticks — neatly divided structures producing a visual sense of density. He said at first it was unconscious: shooting every day with his phone, shooting security training, shooting any fellow worker he happened to see on the street, accumulating day by day, on and off for almost 20 years. When there were so many eras in so many factories, he had not observed in that way; when he discovered it, it was terrifying — even the switches looked spectacular.

points.h: Time as warp, space as weft: a lifetime to understand one society
points.body: The complete thread he worked out was: time as warp, space as weft, the life cycle as the guiding principle, capital's impact on the industrial zone as the axis, forming a comprehensive three-dimensional record including sound, images, video, text and objects. Later he changed methods: starting from the keyword dagong (打工, working for wages), he found ten main keywords on Baidu Scholar, then searched all related terms on Baidu, getting 322, and went into Baidu Images and began screenshotting all of them — this is the internet's understanding of dagong, to be presented together with his own photographic understanding in one huge exhibition space. He said this is how we view the era in an illusory age, while the real era is ignored. He compared himself to a Sherpa: the famous mountaineers are carried by Sherpas, so I'll just be that Sherpa.

terms.def: In the mid-Qing, Cantonese were shipped to America to build railways like piglets; later it meant being cheated by middlemen and drivers who piled on charges during the journey to work.
A researcher takes himself as the object of study, recording the life of the group he belongs to rather than studying an outside ethnic group.
Magnum, the internationally known photography cooperative; Zhan Youbing once studied the work of its photographers one by one on its website.

quotes.text: Back then when you came out to work, it wasn't about riding a train — you felt like you'd gotten into a bandit's den.
This is this era: we view the era from within an illusory age, while the real era is ignored.
I often say that if we use a lifetime to understand a society, the understanding we reach will certainly not be poor; but if we can see a society in a single day, it will certainly be shallow.
